rows.speaker: الكشف
rows.claim: Kashf reconciles the requests by taking the first as asking that the land become continuously habitable and safe for its residents, since it had not been fit for settlement.
rows.anchor: أما بأن المسؤول أولا صلوحه للسكنى بأن يؤمن فيه أهله

rows.speaker: الكشف
rows.claim: Kashf also offers alternatives: safety may be protection from occasional danger, a request for lasting security stated hyperbolically, worldly versus afterlife safety, or a second prayer before the first was answered.
rows.anchor: وأما بالحمل على الاستدامة وتنزيله منزلة العاري عنه مبالغة

rows.speaker: الكشف
rows.claim: Kashf reads the wording as progression: Abraham first asks that this become a safe town, then stresses the request because it is actually fearful; a distressed person's prayer is nearer to being answered.
rows.anchor: وكأنه بنى الكلام على الترقي فطلب أولا أن يكون بلدا آمنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some take the passage as one request retold, while others infer two requests from the changed wording; al-Ālūsī's apparent conclusion is that both townhood and safety were requested.
rows.anchor: فالظاهر أن المسؤول كلا الأمرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī prefers that the townhood request is retold in 14:37 as hearts inclining to Abraham's family for residence, as Ibn ʿAbbās explains, not merely pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: إذ المسؤول هويها إليهم المساكنة كما روى عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another explanation is that security is especially relevant to gratitude, making it apt to mention while rebuking the unbelievers for neglecting God's favors.
rows.anchor: لأن نعمة الا من أدخل في استيجاب الشكر فذكره انسب بمقام تقريع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Abraham narrative is an aside reinforcing the preceding call to gratitude through faith and good works and warning against their opposites; it gently invites the Meccan rejecters.
rows.anchor: واردة على سبيل الاعتراض مقررة لما حث عليه من الشكر بالإيمان والعمل الصالح

rows.speaker: إرشاد العقل السليم
rows.claim: Irshād says the passage heightens the Prophet's astonishment: Quraysh denied special and general blessings, disobeyed Abraham, and replaced the sacred city with ruin despite God's answered prayers.
rows.anchor: وفي إرشاد العقل السليم أن المراد منها تأكيد ماسلف من تعجيبه

rows.speaker: الجحدري وعيسى الثقفي
rows.claim: Al-Jaḥdarī and ʿĪsā al-Thaqafī read the verb with hamza qatʿ and a kasra on the nūn, on the pattern of أكرمني.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجحدري وعيسى الثقفي ( وأجنبني ) بقطع الهمزة وكسر النون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternate form reflects Najdi usage, which has both the light form جنبه and the quadriliteral أجنبَه; the Ḥijāzī form doubles the middle consonant.
rows.anchor: جنبه مخففا وأجنبه رباعيا وأما أهل الحجاز فيقولون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root image of tajannub is being on a different side from another person, then by extension being distant.
rows.anchor: وأصل التجنب أن يكون الرجل في جانب غير ما عليه غيره

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj interprets the prayer as asking God to keep Abraham and his children steadfast in monotheism, Islam, and avoidance of idols, since prophets are protected from unbelief.
rows.anchor: والمراد هنا على ماقال الزجاج طلب الثبات والدوام على ذلك

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī answers that Abraham asked out of humility and to display his need for God's grace in every matter, although he knew God protected him from idolatry.
rows.anchor: الأول أنه عليه السلام وإن كان يعلم أن الله تعالى يعصمه من عبادة الأصنام

rows.speaker: الصوفية
rows.claim: The Sufis distinguish manifest shirk from hidden shirk, attachment of the heart to apparent means; Abraham may be asking for freedom from this subtler attachment.
rows.anchor: والثاني أن الصوفية يقولون : الشرك نوعان ظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī objects that the Sufi account raises the same question: if looking to anything besides God resembles shirk, prophets are already protected from it, so why ask?
rows.anchor: ويرد على هذا الأخير أنه يعود السؤال عليه فيما أظن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī's preferred answer is that prophetic protection is not an innate trait but comes solely through God's enabling grace, so seeking it is meaningful.
rows.anchor: والجواب الصحيح عندي ماقيل : إن عصمة الأنبياء عليهم السلام ليست لأمر طبيعي فيهم

rows.speaker: الله سبحانه
rows.claim: A report says God told Moses not to feel secure from divine plan until he had crossed the bridge; al-Ālūsī offers this as a possible source of the need to seek protection.
rows.anchor: وفي بعض الآثار أن الله سبحانه قال لموسى عليه السلام : ياموسى لاتأمن مكري حتى تجوز الصراط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even people promised Paradise by the truthful Prophet often asked God for it; al-Ālūsī suggests the warning to Moses may explain this practice of seeking what is assured.
rows.anchor: وأنت تعلم أن المبشرين بالجنة على لسان الصادق المصدوق عليه الصلاة والسلام كانوا كثيرا مايسألون الله تعالى الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent meaning of Abraham's sons is his direct offspring; Quraysh's idolatry does not require concluding that his prayer went unanswered.
rows.anchor: والمتبادر من بنيه عليه السلام من كان من صلبه

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some restrict the intended sons to those already alive when Abraham prayed, thereby avoiding the apparent problem posed by later idolatrous descendants.
rows.anchor: بما قاله بعضهم من أن المراد كل من كان موجودا حال الدعاء

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī also allows that the prayer was answered for some descendants but not others, which would not imply any deficiency in Abraham's supplication.
rows.anchor: أو بأن دعاءه استجيب في بعض دون بعض ولا نقص فيه كما قال الإمام

rows.speaker: سفيان بن عيينة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUyayna says Abraham's sons includes all his descendants and claims no Ishmaelite worshipped an image-idol; each people instead set up a stone and circumambulated it.
rows.anchor: وقال سفيان بن عيينة : إن المراد ببنيه مايشمل جميع ذريته عليه السلام

rows.speaker: سفيان بن عيينة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUyayna says people called their installed stone al-dawwār; this is why some disliked saying one circumambulates around the House and preferred the verb ṭāfa bihi.
rows.anchor: وكانوا يدورون به ويسمونه الدوار ولهذا كره غير واحد أن يقال دار بالبيت

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid similarly says no descendant of Abraham worshipped an image-idol, though some worshipped an unfigured object; he distinguishes ṣanam from wathan by whether it is fashioned as an image.
rows.anchor: لم يعبد أحد من ولد إبراهيم عليه السلام صنما وانما عبد بعضهم الوثن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī objects that the Qur'an repeatedly condemns Quraysh for idol worship, which these explanations appear to overlook.
rows.anchor: وليت شعري كيف ذهبت على هذين الجليلين مافي القرآن من قوارع تنعى على قريش عبادة الأصنام

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī calls Mujāhid's distinction weak: Abraham meant worship of anything besides God, and an idol-image and an unfigured idol are equivalent in that respect; the same objection applies to Ibn ʿUyayna.
rows.anchor: قال الإمام بعد نقله كلام مجاهد : إن هذا ليس بقوى لأنه عليه السلام لم يرد بهذا الدعاء

rows.speaker: بعض أصحابنا
rows.claim: Some of al-Ālūsī's school infer that only God distances people from unbelief and brings them near to faith, since Abraham asks God for that distance; al-Ālūsī says the inference is problematic.
rows.anchor: واستدل بعض أصحابنا بالآية على أن التبعيد من الكفر والتقريب من الإيمان ليس إلا من الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun refers to the idols; their causing people to stray is figurative because they are inanimate, while God is the actual misleader.
rows.anchor: اي الاصنام ( اضللن كثيرا من الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement explains Abraham's preceding prayer, and the address “Lord” signals special concern and hope that the request will be answered.
rows.anchor: وهذا تعليل لدعائه عليه السلام السابق وصدر بالنداء إظهارا للاعتناء به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “From me” may be partitive by simile, making the follower like an inseparable part of Abraham, or connective, meaning attached to him in religion.
rows.anchor: يحتمل أن تكون ( من ) تبعيضية على التشبيه

rows.speaker: الشريفي
rows.claim: Al-Sharīf's commentary explains connective min as marking the follower's connection to Abraham rather than literal origin; al-Ālūsī favors a specific implied relation over a general one.
rows.anchor: كذا في حواشي شرح المفتاح للشريفي يعني أن مجرورها ليس مبدأ أو منشأ لنفس ما قبلها

rows.speaker: الجلال السيوطي
rows.claim: Al-Suyūṭī says the connective min in “you are from me” has a specific understood relation, glossed as being connected to and deriving status from the speaker.
rows.anchor: كما قاله الجلال السيوطي في بيان الخبر من أن ( مني ) فيه خبر المبتدأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following Abraham means following his call to monotheism and the religion of Islam.
rows.anchor: منهم فيما أدعو إليه من التوحيد وملة الإسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Disobeyed me” means did not follow Abraham; this wording implies he continued preaching, so nonfollowers failed through disobedience rather than lack of access to the message.
rows.anchor: والتعبير عنه بالعصيان كما قيل للايذان بأنه عليه السلام مستمر على الدعوة

rows.speaker: البحر
rows.claim: Al-Baḥr notes a semantic antithesis between following Abraham and disobeying him, since following is obedience.
rows.anchor: وفي البحر أن بين الاتباع والعصيان طباقا معنويا لأن الاتباع طاعة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some commentators supply an omitted clause: “whoever disobeys me, I will not pray against him,” followed by Abraham's appeal to God's forgiveness and mercy.
rows.anchor: وفي الكلام على ما أشار إليه البعض حذف والتقدير ومن عصاني فلا أدعو عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse indicates that forgiveness of shirk can be possible; al-Ālūsī cites al-Nawawī's account that it was permitted for earlier communities but barred in Islamic law.
rows.anchor: وفي الآية دليل على أن الشرك يجوز أن يغفر ولا إشكال في ذلك بناء على ما قال النووي

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddī, among those who deny that any dispensation allowed forgiveness of shirk, takes the promise as applying after repentance.
rows.anchor: فمنهم من ذهب إلى أن المراد غفور رحيم بعد التوبة ونسب ذلك إلى السدي

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: One report from Muqātil restricts “disobedience” to sins below shirk, though al-Ālūsī says this ignores the wording's unrestricted contrast.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من ذهب إلى تقييد العصيان بما دون الشرك وغفل عما تقتضيه المعادلة وروي ذلك عن مقاتل

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Another report from Muqātil says a person persisting in unbelief may be forgiven by being moved from unbelief to faith and guided to what is right.
rows.anchor: وفي رواية أخرى عنه أنه قال : إن المعنى ومن عصاني بإقامته على الكفر

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another explanation is that God may spare a person who persists in shirk by delaying punishment; it compares this to God's forgiveness despite people's wrongdoing.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من قال : المعنى ومن لم يتبعني فيما أدعو إليه من التوحيد

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some take the statement literally and say Abraham spoke before learning that God does not forgive shirk; this is no fault, since reason allows it and a prophet need not know every revealed proof at once.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من قال : إن الكلام على ظاهره وكان ذلك منه عليه السلام قبل أن يعلم

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī rejects the narrower readings and argues that the unrestricted phrase concerns intercession for major sinners before repentance; he then extends that precedent to the Prophet through the command to follow Abraham.
rows.anchor: والإمام لم يرتض أكثر هذه الأوجه وجعل هذا الكلام منه عليه السلام شفاعة في إسقاط العقاب عن أهل الكبائر قبل التوبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī signals that al-Rāzī's intercession argument is unpersuasive and points readers to an earlier discussion for the relevant answer.
rows.anchor: وهو كما ترى وقد مر لك ماينفعك في هذا المقام فتذكر

rows.speaker: البحر
rows.claim: Al-Baḥr says the repeated address seeks an answer and refuge in God, and the plural pronoun reflects Abraham's mention of his sons in the prior verse.
rows.anchor: قال في البحر كرر النداء رغبة في الإجابة والالتجاء إليه تعالى وأتى بضمير الجماعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects that explanation because it would also predict a plural address in 14:36; the plural here instead suits the descendants who are the subject of the settlement and its preparatory prayer.
rows.anchor: وتعقب بأن ذلك يقتضي ضمير الجماعة في ( رب إنهن ) الخ مع أنه جيء فيه بضمير الواحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min may be partitive, with the phrase functioning as the object by interpretation, or the object may be omitted and the phrase serve as its adjective; min may then be partitive or explanatory.
rows.anchor: بمعنى بعض وهي في تأويل المفعول به أي أسكنت بعض ذريتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some call min extra following al-Akhfash, but al-Ālūsī dismisses that analysis as unacceptable to sound judgment.
rows.anchor: زائدة على مذهب الأخفش لايرتضيه سليم البصيرة كما لايخفى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The settled descendant is Ishmael and the descendants he would have; settling him peacefully entails settling them, while the explicit plural purpose clause motivates the broader reference.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالمسكن إسماعيل عليه السلام ومن سيولد له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Settlement applies literally to Ishmael and figuratively to his offspring; interpreters who disallow combining literal and figurative senses must posit a general metaphor.
rows.anchor: الاسكان له حقيقة ولأولاده مجاز فمن لم يجوز الجمع بين الحقيقة والمجاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī recounts that Hagar, an Egyptian Copt given to Abraham by Sarah, bore Ishmael; after Sarah became jealous, Abraham took mother and child to the empty, waterless Meccan valley with dates and water.
rows.anchor: وذلك أن هاجر أم إسماعيل كانت أمه من القبط لسارة فوهبتها من إبراهيم عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hagar repeatedly asked why Abraham was leaving them in a deserted valley; when she learned God had commanded it, she trusted that He would not abandon them.
rows.anchor: الله أمرك بهذا قال : نعم ( 1 ) قالت : إذن لايضيعنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham left until hidden from them, turned toward the House, then prayed the words of this verse with raised hands; the House then stood on a rise where floodwaters passed to either side.
rows.anchor: استقبل بوجهه البيت وكان إذ ذاك مرتفعا من الأرض كالرابية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When their water ran out, Hagar's thirsty infant writhed; she ran between Ṣafā and Marwa seven times searching for help, which the account gives as the origin of the seven circuits of saʿy.
rows.anchor: ففعلت ذلك سبع مرات ولذلك سعى الناس بينهما سبعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An angel dug with his heel at Zamzam until water appeared; Hagar drank and nursed Ishmael while the spring flowed.
rows.anchor: فإذا هي بالملك عند موضع زمزم فبحث بعقبه حتى ظهر الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angel reassured Hagar that God would not abandon them and that the boy and his father would build God's House there; later a Jurhum party found the water, settled with her by exchanging milk for access, and married Ishmael to one of their women.
rows.anchor: لاتخافي الضيعة فان ههنا بيت الله تعالى يبنيه هذا الغلام وأبوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The valley is Mecca; “not possessing cultivation” intensifies “uncultivated,” meaning it was unfit for farming, as in the phrase “an Arabic Qur'an with no crookedness.”
rows.anchor: ووصفه بذلك دون غير مزروع للمبالغة لأن المعنى ليس صالحا للزرع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording is compared with Qur'an 39:28, “an Arabic Qur'an with no crookedness,” where the construction likewise intensifies the negation.
rows.anchor: قوله تعالى : ( قرآنا عربيا غير ذي عوج ) وكان

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya explains that Abraham omitted “without water” because he knew God would provide water for Ishmael and Hagar and would not neglect them.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية : وإنما لم يصفه عليه السلام بالخلو عن الماء

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān argues that saying the valley had no crops already entails that it had no water, since crops cannot exist without water.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو حيان بعد نقله وقد يقال : إن انتفاء كونه ذا زرع

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say water was not Abraham's chief concern because floodwater could be stored; he chiefly sought fruit, and the description emphasizes the family's complete dependence on God's provision.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم : ان طلب الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī takes “at Your inviolable House” as an adverbial phrase modifying “I settled”; Abū al-Baqā instead calls it an adjective of “valley” or an apposition.
rows.anchor: ظرف لأسكنت كقولك : صليت بمكة عند الركن

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqā analyzes the phrase as an adjective of “valley” or as an apposition; al-Ālūsī prefers the adverbial attachment because it highlights settlement beside God's sanctuary.
rows.anchor: وزعم أبو البقاء أنه صفة ( واد ) أو بدل منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The House is called inviolable because God forbade violating or slighting it; alternatively, it has always been protected and feared by tyrants, or the flood was prevented from overtaking it, hence its name al-ʿAtīq.
rows.anchor: معنى كون البيت محرما أن الله تعالى حرم التعرض له والتهاون به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects the explanation that it is called inviolable because visitors forbid themselves otherwise lawful acts; Abraham calls it a House in reference either to its former state or to its future construction.
rows.anchor: وأبعد من قال إنه سمي محرما لأن الزائرين يحرمون على أنفسهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām is purposive, with an implicit أن making the verb subjunctive, and the phrase attaches to “I settled”; repeating “Our Lord” emphasizes establishing prayer, the pillar of religion.
rows.anchor: لأن يقيموا فللام جارة والفعل منصوب بأن مضمرة بعدها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The barren valley and sacred House imply that Abraham settled them there for worship alone: establishing prayer, cultivating the sanctuary through remembrance and worship, and seeking God's mercy and nearness.
rows.anchor: ما أسكنتهم بهذا الوادي البلقع الخالي من كل مرتفق ومرتزق

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Mālik holds that a purpose clause implies exclusivity and uses “that you may ride them” in 16:8 to argue that the animals are not for eating.
rows.anchor: وعن مالك أن التعليل يفيد الحصر فقد استدل بقوله تعالى : ( لتركبوها )

rows.speaker: الكشف
rows.claim: Kashf derives the exclusivity from an implied later verb, “I settled them in this settlement so that they would establish prayer”; the intervening second “Our Lord” shows the phrase does not modify the stated verb.
rows.anchor: وفي الكشف أن استفادة الحصر من تقدير محذوف مؤخر يتعلق به الجار والمجرور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī prefers deriving exclusivity from the sequence: barren land rules out farming, the House establishes worship, and the purpose clause identifies prayer; the repeated address is parenthetical emphasis, so no omitted verb is needed.
rows.anchor: واختار بعضهم ماذكرناه أولا في وجه الاستفادة وقال : انه معنى لطيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A less plausible reading treats the lām as an imperative asking God to enable them to pray; Ibn al-Jawzī's still more remote proposal attaches it to “keep me and my sons away from idolatry.”
rows.anchor: وقيل : اللام لام الأمر والفعل مجزوم بها والمراد هو الدعاء لهم

rows.speaker: البحر
rows.claim: The plural “they may establish” indicates that God informed Abraham that Ishmael would have descendants in that place.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله : ( ليقيموا ) بضمير الجمع على مافي البحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Hearts from among people” means some hearts, so the request does not entail that all nations crowd the family; the author assumes the prayer was answered and the generic plural can denote everyone.
rows.anchor: أي أفئدة من أفئدتهم ( تهوي إليهم ( أي تسرع إليهم شوقا وودادا

rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: Ibn Jubayr says that if Abraham had asked for the hearts of all people, Jews and Christians would have made pilgrimage to the House.
rows.anchor: وروى عن ابن جبير أنه قال : لو قال عليه السلام : أفئدة الناس لحجت البيت اليهود والنصارى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says Ibn Jubayr's reading is not apt if Abraham asked for hearts to incline to the family for residence rather than to the House for pilgrimage; the two readings can nevertheless coexist.
rows.anchor: وتعقب بأنه غير مناسب للمقام إذا المسؤول توجيه القلوب إليهم للمساكنة معهم

rows.speaker: عكرمة وطاوس وعطاء بن أبي رباح
rows.claim: Al-Ḥakam says he asked ʿIkrima, Ṭāwūs, and ʿAṭāʾ about the phrase; they answered that hearts incline to the House and people come to it, glossing this as love of Mecca for pilgrimage.
rows.anchor: عن الحكم قال : سألت عكرمة وطاوسا وعطاء ابن أبي رباح عن هذه الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some interpret the request as directing hearts to the House; although this differs from the apparent reference to Abraham's family, the pilgrimage reading need not conflict with a request for people to settle with them.
rows.anchor: على أن بعضهم جعل هذا دعاء بتوجيه القلوب إلى البيت

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān doubts that min marks a point of origin, since there is no verb here from which hearts could begin toward an endpoint.
rows.anchor: واعترضه أبو حيان بأنه لايظهر كونها للابتداء لأنه لافعل هنا يبتدأ فيه

rows.speaker: بعض الأجلة
rows.claim: A senior scholar replies that the verb “incline” supplies the motion: hearts begin their inclination from people toward the family, as indicated by “to them.”
rows.anchor: وتعقبه بعض الاجلة بقوله : وفيه بحث فان فعل الهوى للأفئدة يبتدأ به

rows.speaker: مولانا الشهاب
rows.claim: Al-Shihāb favors min of origin: partitivity adds no information because everyone knows a person's heart is part of them; the phrase instead depicts inclination as arising from the whole person.
rows.anchor: وذكر مولانا الشهاب في توجيه الابتداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “my bones are weak from me” in 19:4 illustrates the point that min of origin can identify the source of an attribute without stating a meaningful partitive fact.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل : إن جميع معاني ( من ) دائرة على الابتداء والتبعيض هنا لايظهر فيه فائدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Afʾida is the first object of “make” and the plural of fuʾād; lexicographers gloss it as the heart, called fuʾād when its burning or glowing quality is considered.
rows.anchor: والأفئدة مفعول أول لاجعل وهو جمع فؤاد وفسروه على مافي البحر وغيره بالقلب
